CD8 T-cell exhaustion linked with CAR T-cell failure can be mitigated by a non-alpha IL2 receptor agonist

Arita K, Dai E, Li X et al. · 2026 Oct 23
Study Type: Preclinical translational study (patient tumour scRNA-seq, in vitro rechallenge model, in vivo xenograft model). Not a clinical trial.
Key Question: Does chronic antigen stimulation drive CD8 CART19 exhaustion in rrLBCL, and can a non-alpha IL2 receptor agonist (pegenzileukin) prevent it?
Key Findings:
  • scRNA-seq of post-CART19 progression tumours showed clonally expanded, proliferating CART19 cells with dysfunction signatures in a subset of patients, consistent with ongoing tumour engagement rather than CAR T-cell absence.
  • In vitro, serial tumour rechallenge caused loss of tumour control, T-cell dysfunction and reduced IL2 signalling; pegenzileukin restored T-cell expansion and tumour control.
  • In an in vivo model derived from a post-CART19 progression tumour, CART19 alone gave transient response then progression with CNS relapse; CART19 plus pegenzileukin achieved complete tumour eradication.
Clinical Relevance: Supports exhaustion as a targetable failure mechanism after CAR-T for rrLBCL, a major unmet need given limited options at post-CAR-T relapse in the NHS.
Limitations: Evidence is entirely preclinical, with efficacy shown in a single patient-derived model and no human safety or efficacy data.

Thrombin-mediated AutoRegulation of FVIII-mimetic antibodies enabling dynamic control of the hemostatic response

Muczynski V, Smith A, Baccaro A et al. · 2026 Oct 23
Study Type: Preclinical experimental study (in vitro assays and murine in vivo models); no human data.
Key Question: Can adding a thrombin-cleavable hinge peptide to emicizumab create a self-limiting FVIII-mimetic antibody that retains haemostatic efficacy while reducing thrombotic risk, particularly with aPCC co-exposure?
Key Findings:
  • AR-emicizumab matched parental emicizumab for EC50 of FVIII-mimetic activity and correction of blood loss in haemophilia A mice.
  • Under supra-physiological thrombin exposure, AR-emicizumab was proteolytically inactivated (parental drug unaffected), significantly attenuating the excess thrombin peak seen with emicizumab plus aPCC in thrombin generation assays.
  • In vivo, AR-emicizumab prevented platelet-consumptive coagulopathy and reduced microvascular pulmonary thrombosis versus the parental molecule, without altering systemic antibody levels. Specific effect sizes were not reported in the abstract.
Clinical Relevance: Thrombotic microangiopathy and thrombosis with emicizumab plus aPCC remain a concern for UK clinicians managing breakthrough bleeds in inhibitor patients, so this is an early proof-of-concept for a potentially safer next-generation agent.
Limitations: Findings are preclinical only; safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy of the thrombin-cleavable construct in humans are untested.

Immunologic and Plasma-Dependent Mechanisms of Chronic Hemolysis and Hyperhemolysis in Sickle Cell Disease

Hillis LK, Branch DR, Pendergrast J · 2026 Oct 23
Study Type: Narrative review (with a proposed mechanistic model drawing on the authors' own and others' investigations). No systematic search methodology is stated in the abstract.
Key Question: What immunologic and plasma-dependent mechanisms drive chronic haemolysis and acute hyperhaemolysis in sickle cell disease?
Key Findings:
  • Sickle red cell clearance is immune-regulated, involving altered membrane markers (phosphatidylserine, mannose, CD47, CD95/Fas), plasma opsonins (including IgG, C3b, Gas6, MFG-E8) and their macrophage receptors.
  • Proposed model: chronic haemolysis is predominantly extravascular (erythrophagocytosis), whereas acute events, including post-transfusion hyperhaemolysis syndrome (HHS), shift towards intravascular haemolysis via membrane attack complex assembly, Fas-mediated erythronecroptosis and heme-mediated ferroptosis.
  • Mechanisms by which transfusion may accelerate these pathways and precipitate HHS are discussed.
Clinical Relevance: The proposed complement- and cell-death-based mechanisms of HHS may inform future therapeutic targets (e.g., complement inhibition) and transfusion strategies for SCD patients in UK practice, where HHS remains difficult to manage.
Limitations: As a narrative review presenting a hypothesis-generating model, it provides no quantitative clinical data, and the proposed model has not been validated clinically.

Initial fixed low-versus moderate-dose hydroxyurea assignment in the long-term follow-up of the SPRINT cohort

Iguda SM, Abdullahi SU, Idris IM et al. · 2026 Oct 26
Study Type: Pragmatic long-term follow-up of a randomised trial cohort (SPRINT); post-hoc observational extension, not a new randomised comparison.
Key Question: Does initial fixed low-dose versus moderate-dose hydroxyurea affect long-term recurrent stroke and mortality in children with sickle cell disease and prior stroke?
Key Findings:
  • Over 4.9 years of follow-up, recurrent stroke and all-cause mortality did not differ significantly between low and moderate initial fixed-dose arms.
  • Events clustered in the first year after assignment.
  • Effect sizes, confidence intervals, event numbers and sample size are not reported in the abstract.
Clinical Relevance: Supports the view that fixed-dose hydroxyurea may be a pragmatic option, particularly in resource-limited settings, though UK practice (dose escalation to maximum tolerated dose, with transfusion for secondary stroke prevention) is unlikely to change on this evidence alone.
Limitations: The abstract lacks quantitative data, and population, setting and dosing details are unspecified (SPRINT context is inferred); non-significance may reflect insufficient power rather than true equivalence.

Molecular Underpinnings and Prevalence of Donor Cell-Derived Hematologic Neoplasms among Spanish Transplantation Centers

Gabarros-Subira M, Pomares H, Beas F et al. · 2026 Oct 26
Study Type: Nationwide multicentre retrospective cohort study with molecular characterisation (24 Spanish centres)
Key Question: How common are donor cell-derived haematologic neoplasms (DDHN) after allo-HSCT, and what molecular mechanisms drive them?
Key Findings:
  • Prevalence was 0.28% among 8,465 allo-HSCTs (2013–2022), significantly higher after related-donor than unrelated-donor transplants (0.41% vs 0.06%, p=0.0026). Median latency was 56 months; 87% of the 39 cases were MDS (51%) or AML (36%).
  • Of 33 cases with molecular data, 10 carried pathogenic/likely pathogenic germline variants (DDX41 n=7, CEBPA n=2, CHEK2 n=1), all in related-donor transplants.
  • Donor-derived clonal hematopoiesis was confirmed in only one case (U2AF1).
Clinical Relevance: Supports germline testing at diagnosis in patients being considered for allo-HSCT, with cascade testing of candidate related donors, which is relevant to UK donor selection and genomic testing pathways.
Limitations: Retrospective design with likely under-ascertainment of DDHN, and molecular data were unavailable for 6 of the 39 cases.

Splicing Factor Mutations in Myeloid Malignancies

Cazzola M, Ogawa S · 2026 Oct 26
Study Type: Narrative review (no original data; abstract reports no systematic methodology).
Key Question: What is currently understood about the biology, genotype-phenotype associations and clinical implications of recurrent splicing factor mutations in myeloid malignancies, particularly MDS?
Key Findings:
  • Splicing factor mutations, first described in 2011, are among the most frequent genetic lesions in MDS and related dysplastic myeloid neoplasms, implicating aberrant RNA splicing as a core pathogenetic pathway.
  • Mutation-specific splicing effects and strong genotype-phenotype associations are established, and SF mutations are now incorporated into current disease classification and prognostic models.
  • The mechanisms driving positive clonal selection and genotype-phenotype associations remain poorly understood; co-mutations, clonal architecture, ageing and the marrow microenvironment modify disease expression.
Clinical Relevance: SF mutation status already informs classification and risk stratification in MDS, so UK haematologists should understand its biological basis when interpreting NGS myeloid panel results, though therapeutic translation remains unrealised.
Limitations: As a narrative review, it offers expert synthesis rather than new evidence, and the abstract gives no quantitative data or specific therapeutic findings.

Multi-omics reveals evolution from CD7-negative T cell dysregulation to EBV-positive LPD after CD7 CAR-T therapy

Huang M, Jiang Y, Ye F et al. · 2026 Oct 28
Study Type: Translational/mechanistic study using multi-omic spatial profiling (snRNA-seq, ATAC-seq, Stereo-seq) of patient tissue; sample sizes not stated in abstract.
Key Question: What are the immune and molecular mechanisms driving EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorder after CD7 CAR-T therapy (PCLD)?
Key Findings:
  • Infiltrating T cells in PCLD are CD7-negative, with limited proliferative capacity and impaired anti-EBV activity, consistent with loss of effective viral surveillance.
  • IDO1-high macrophages (Macro_IDO1) form spatially organised immunosuppressive niches that exclude T cells and are enriched for inhibitory signalling, including PD-1/PD-L1.
  • Uncontrolled EBV infection of B cells drives plasmacytic differentiation, sustained proliferation and microenvironmental remodelling. PCLD was compared against PTLD, EBV-negative DLBCL and normal lymph nodes.
Clinical Relevance: As CD7 CAR-T is explored for T-cell malignancies, clinicians should anticipate EBV reactivation and LPD as a distinct post-therapy risk, with PD-1/IDO1 pathways emerging as candidate intervention targets.
Limitations: Abstract reports no cohort size, incidence, clinical outcomes or interventional data, so generalisability and therapeutic implications cannot be assessed.

Low Incidence of Cryptic Genetic Marrow Failure in Pediatric Severe Aplastic Anemia Following Negative Clinical Workup

de Jong JLO, Reed HD, Gaviria Garrido M et al. · 2026 Oct 28
Study Type: Retrospective cohort study (single analysis of paediatric SAA patients with targeted enhanced whole exome sequencing).
Key Question: In children with severe aplastic anaemia (SAA) and a negative standard clinical/laboratory workup for inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFS), is waiting for germline genetic testing justified?
Key Findings:
  • Of 149 patients with complete clinical data, 113 (75.8%) had no IBMFS features; none carried pathogenic or likely pathogenic IBMFS variants.
  • Among 36 patients (24.2%) with at least one suggestive clinical finding, one had a pathogenic heterozygous *SAMD9L* variant with a consistent history; another had two *ERCC6L2* pathogenic variants, but phasing (and so affected status) was undetermined.
Clinical Relevance: Supports starting definitive immunosuppressive or transplant-pathway treatment without delay for genetic results in children with a clean comprehensive workup, which is relevant to UK paediatric SAA pathways.
Limitations: Retrospective design; sequencing was IBMFS-gene-targeted, so non-exomic or novel genetic causes may have been missed.
